title: Skin Biochemistry and Nutrition
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Skin is built from proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates that depend on vitamins and minerals, so it often shows the first visible sign of a nutritional or metabolic defect. This chapter follows collagen synthesis step by step, links vitamin C, copper, niacin, vitamin A, zinc, biotin, riboflavin, and essential fatty acids to specific skin findings, traces vitamin D from the epidermis to the kidney, and explains barrier lipids, sebum, and dermal glycosaminoglycans. It ends with skin signs of systemic metabolism: xanthomas that point to a lipoprotein disorder and the photosensitive blisters of porphyria cutanea tarda. Board questions usually describe a lesion and ask for the enzyme, cofactor, or pathway step behind it.
prerequisites: Layers of the epidermis and dermis and the dermal-epidermal junction (IN-1)
Protein synthesis on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, the Golgi, and secretion
Vitamin cofactor roles (NAD+, FAD, pyridoxal phosphate, biotin)
Lipoprotein classes, apolipoproteins, and lipoprotein lipase
Steps of heme synthesis and the enzymes that catalyze them

connections.how: The same collagen synthesis steps build bone, tendon, and ligament, so osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome affect both skin and skeleton.
Vitamin D made in skin becomes a hormone only after hepatic and renal hydroxylation, and the renal step is controlled by PTH, phosphate, and FGF23.
Xanthomas are visible deposits of the same lipoproteins that drive atherosclerosis and, with severe hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatitis.
Porphyria cutanea tarda is a defect of heme synthesis, and iron overload is one of its strongest triggers.
Malabsorption, carcinoid tumors, and intestinal transport defects such as Hartnup disease and acrodermatitis enteropathica present with skin signs.

sections.title: Collagen synthesis and the defect at each step

blocks.text: Collagen is the main structural protein of the dermis, and type I collagen supplies most of its tensile strength. Each molecule is three left-handed alpha chains wound together into a right-handed triple helix, and each chain is a repeat of Gly-X-Y in which X is often proline and Y is often hydroxyproline. Glycine must occupy every third position because it is the only amino acid small enough to fit in the crowded center of the helix.

blocks.title: Collagen synthesis from gene to cross-linked fibril
steps: Pre-pro-alpha chains made on rough ER
Proline and lysine hydroxylated (vitamin C, Fe2+, O2)
Selected hydroxylysines glycosylated (galactose, glucose)
C-propeptides align three chains; triple helix zips
Procollagen packaged in Golgi and secreted
Procollagen peptidases cleave N- and C-propeptides
Tropocollagen self-assembles into fibrils
Lysyl oxidase (copper) cross-links fibrils
blocks.caption: The first five steps occur inside the fibroblast and the last three outside it. A failure at any step yields weak or deficient collagen.

blocks.text: Inside the cell, prolyl 4-hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase act on the chains before the helix forms. Both are dioxygenases that use O2 and alpha-ketoglutarate and hold Fe2+ at the active site; ascorbate (vitamin C) reduces the iron back to Fe2+ when it becomes oxidized. Hydroxyproline stabilizes the helix through hydrogen bonding, so underhydroxylated chains fold poorly at body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F), and are largely degraded instead of secreted. Hydroxylysine is needed for glycosylation and later for stable cross-links. Disulfide bonds between the C-propeptides bring three chains into register, and the helix then forms from the C-terminus toward the N-terminus.

Outside the cell, removal of the propeptides converts soluble procollagen to tropocollagen, which packs into staggered fibrils. Lysyl oxidase then oxidizes lysine and hydroxylysine side chains to aldehydes (allysine) that condense into covalent cross-links between molecules. Fibrils without these cross-links assemble but tear easily.

blocks.title: Predicting the defect from the failed step
rows: Unstable helix, less collagen secreted; fragile vessels and poor healing
Few stable cross-links; hyperextensible skin, scoliosis
Osteogenesis imperfecta (glycine substitution in type I collagen)
Abnormal or reduced type I collagen; brittle bones, blue sclerae
Disorganized fibrils; very fragile, sagging skin
Weak fibrils and elastin; vascular and skin fragility
blocks.caption: No common human disease maps to the hydroxylysine glycosylation step. Classic and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are instead caused by mutations in type V and type III collagen genes.

blocks.predict: A glycine-to-cysteine substitution in one type I collagen chain still lets the chain be made. Why can a single substituted allele disrupt most of the collagen?
blocks.explain: Each molecule contains two alpha1(I) chains, so with one mutant COL1A1 allele about three of four molecules contain at least one abnormal chain, and a bulky residue in the helix center blocks normal folding of the whole molecule (a dominant negative effect).
blocks.check: Compare with the glycine requirement and the triple helix formation row of the table.

blocks.text: Scurvy is the clinical result of failed collagen hydroxylation. The body has no way to make ascorbate, and stores are depleted after about one to three months of an intake near zero, so scurvy appears where fruit and vegetable intake is near zero, as in some older adults living alone, people with alcohol use disorder, and those on highly selective diets.

Every classic finding follows from weak collagen in a particular place. Capillaries around hair follicles have little supporting tissue, so they rupture into perifollicular hemorrhages, often on the legs where hydrostatic pressure is highest. Follicles also become plugged with keratin, and the hair shafts inside them coil into corkscrew hairs. Gum tissue turns over rapidly and is under mechanical stress, so it becomes swollen, spongy, and bleeds easily, especially where teeth are present. New wounds heal poorly because fibroblasts cannot lay down stable collagen, and old scars can break down because collagen is normally being remodeled. Bleeding into joints and under the periosteum causes pain. Platelet counts and clotting tests are normal; the bleeding comes from weak vessel support, not from a coagulation defect. Anemia is common, both from blood loss and because ascorbate normally keeps dietary iron in the absorbable ferrous form.

Menkes disease reaches the same final step through copper. It is an X-linked recessive disorder of the ATP7A gene, which encodes a copper-transporting ATPase that moves copper out of intestinal cells into the blood and into the secretory pathway of other cells. Copper is absorbed into enterocytes but trapped there, so serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low and copper-dependent enzymes throughout the body run short. Wilson disease involves the related ATP7B transporter in the liver and causes copper overload instead.

blocks.title: Copper enzymes and the Menkes findings they explain
rows: Tortuous, fragile arteries; loose skin; bladder diverticula
Thiol oxidation in hair keratin (enzyme not characterized)
Final step of the electron transport chain
blocks.caption: Affected boys usually present in the first months of life, and the classic severe form is often fatal in early childhood.

blocks.text: Scurvy blocks an intracellular step, so less collagen is secreted, while Menkes blocks an extracellular step, so collagen is secreted but poorly cross-linked. Both cause vascular fragility, but only Menkes adds kinky hair, hypopigmentation, and neurodegeneration from loss of other copper enzymes.

sections.title: Pellagra and the tryptophan to niacin pathway

blocks.text: Niacin (nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, vitamin B3) is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+, the carriers of hydride ions in hundreds of oxidation-reduction reactions. Deficiency therefore harms tissues with high turnover and high energy demand: the skin, the lining of the gut, and the brain. Pellagra is classically remembered as dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, and untreated it ends in death.

The dermatitis is photosensitive. It begins like a sunburn on exposed skin, then becomes dark, thick, scaly, and sharply bordered, as on the backs of the hands and in a band around the neck (Casal necklace). The exact cause of photosensitivity is not fully settled. A leading explanation is that UV-damaged keratinocytes depend on NAD+, the substrate of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, to repair DNA, so a low NAD+ supply impairs repair and survival after sun exposure.

Niacin comes from the diet or is made from tryptophan, and every cause of pellagra either removes tryptophan or blocks this pathway. About 60 mg of tryptophan yields 1 mg of niacin, and the pathway needs vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate for kynureninase) and riboflavin (FAD for kynurenine monooxygenase).

steps: Dietary tryptophan absorbed (lost in Hartnup disease)
Tryptophan diverted to serotonin (carcinoid syndrome)
Kynurenine formed in the liver
FAD-dependent and B6-dependent steps (isoniazid depletes B6)
Quinolinic acid to nicotinic acid mononucleotide
NAD+ and NADP+
blocks.caption: Any step that removes tryptophan or its cofactors lowers NAD+ supply.

blocks.title: Causes of pellagra by mechanism
rows: Corn is low in tryptophan and its niacin is bound in a form poorly released by digestion; alkali processing (nixtamalization) frees it
Autosomal recessive defect of the neutral amino acid transporter (B0AT1, SLC6A19) in the small intestine and proximal tubule; tryptophan is poorly absorbed and lost in urine (neutral aminoaciduria)
Tumor cells convert a large share of tryptophan, normally about 1%, to serotonin, leaving little for niacin
Forms an inactive compound with pyridoxal and depletes vitamin B6, blocking the B6-dependent step
Low intake and absorption of niacin, tryptophan, B6, and B2
blocks.caption: Dietary niacin bypasses the pathway, so pellagra needs both a low niacin and a low tryptophan supply.

blocks.title: Worked example: carcinoid tumor with a rash
blocks.text: A patient with liver metastases from a small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor has flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing, then develops a scaly, dark rash on the backs of the hands and the neck. Step 1: hepatic metastases release serotonin directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing liver inactivation, which explains flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm. Step 2: the tumor consumes a large fraction of dietary tryptophan to make serotonin. Step 3: less tryptophan enters the kynurenine pathway, so endogenous niacin and NAD+ synthesis falls. Step 4: NAD+-dependent repair in sun-damaged keratinocytes fails, producing photosensitive pellagra. Urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the serotonin breakdown product, is elevated, confirming the diversion.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with Hartnup disease develop pellagra-like dermatitis even though serum levels of most other amino acids stay near normal?
blocks.explain: Other amino acids are absorbed as dipeptides and tripeptides through a separate peptide transporter, which keeps protein nutrition adequate, but free tryptophan uptake through the neutral transporter is reduced and renal loss continues, so niacin synthesis falls when dietary niacin is marginal.

sections.title: Skin signs of vitamin A, zinc, biotin, riboflavin, and essential fatty acid deficiency

blocks.text: Each of these nutrients has a specific job in renewing epithelium, so the pattern and site of the skin change point to the missing one. Retinoic acid, the active form of vitamin A, binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors that guide keratinocyte differentiation and mucus cell development. Without it, epithelia undergo squamous metaplasia and overkeratinize, so follicles fill with keratin plugs (follicular hyperkeratosis, called phrynoderma) and the skin becomes dry and rough (xerosis). The same defect in the eye causes night blindness, conjunctival xerosis with Bitot spots, and corneal damage.

Zinc is a cofactor for more than 300 enzymes and a structural part of zinc finger transcription factors, so it is critical where cells divide quickly. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is the inherited form, an autosomal recessive defect in the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 (SLC39A4), and it typically appears when an infant is weaned from breast milk, which carries zinc in a more absorbable form. Acquired deficiency follows malabsorption, alcohol use disorder, or zinc-free parenteral nutrition. The dermatitis is red, scaly, and sometimes blistered around the mouth, eyes, and anus and on the hands and feet, with alopecia, diarrhea, poor wound healing, and loss of taste.

Biotin is the carboxyl carrier for the four carboxylases (acetyl-CoA, pyruvate, propionyl-CoA, and 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA). Deficiency comes from large intakes of raw egg white, whose avidin binds biotin, from inherited biotinidase deficiency, or rarely from long parenteral nutrition without biotin. Loss of acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity limits fatty acid synthesis for barrier lipids, giving a scaly periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, and conjunctivitis that closely resemble zinc deficiency.

Riboflavin forms FAD and FMN. Deficiency shows first where epithelium is thin and constantly moving, at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis), the lips (cheilosis), and the tongue (glossitis), with seborrheic-like dermatitis. Essential fatty acid deficiency removes linoleic acid, which is built into the special ceramides of the stratum corneum (C06), so the barrier leaks water and the skin becomes dry, scaly, and slow to heal.

rows: Periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, poor healing
Diarrhea, loss of taste, onset at weaning

blocks.caption: Zinc and biotin deficiency look alike in the skin; history (weaning, egg white, parenteral nutrition) and measured levels separate them.

sections.title: Vitamin D synthesis in skin and what limits it

blocks.text: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) can be made entirely in the body, which is why calcitriol is classed as a hormone. The starting material is 7-dehydrocholesterol, the immediate precursor of cholesterol, held in keratinocyte membranes with the highest amounts in the stratum basale and stratum spinosum. Ultraviolet B light (about 290 to 315 nm) opens its B ring to form previtamin D3, which then rearranges by a heat-dependent isomerization at skin temperature over hours to days into cholecalciferol. Vitamin D binding protein carries it from the skin into the circulation.

blocks.title: From 7-dehydrocholesterol to calcitriol
steps: 7-dehydrocholesterol in basal and spinous keratinocytes
UVB opens B ring: previtamin D3
Thermal isomerization: cholecalciferol (D3)
Carried on vitamin D binding protein to liver
Liver 25-hydroxylase: 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol)
Kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase (proximal tubule): calcitriol
Calcitriol raises gut Ca2+ and phosphate absorption
blocks.caption: Dietary D2 and D3 join the pathway at the liver step. Only the renal step is tightly regulated.

blocks.text: The two hydroxylations differ in control. Hepatic 25-hydroxylation is loosely regulated and depends mostly on substrate supply, so 25-hydroxyvitamin D, with a half-life of about two to three weeks, is the best measure of body vitamin D status. Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is the control point: PTH and low phosphate stimulate it, while FGF23, high phosphate, and calcitriol itself suppress it, and 24-hydroxylase diverts both forms toward inactive products. Because of this control, calcitriol is often normal or even high in early vitamin D deficiency, as rising PTH drives the remaining substrate through the kidney.

Anything that keeps UVB photons from reaching 7-dehydrocholesterol lowers production. Melanin absorbs UVB, so deeply pigmented skin needs several times longer exposure to make the same amount. At high latitude, in winter, and early or late in the day, sunlight passes obliquely through more atmosphere and ozone absorbs most UVB; above about 35 to 40 degrees of latitude little vitamin D is made in winter months. Sunscreen absorbs UVB by design and, applied properly, greatly reduces synthesis, as do clothing, window glass, and staying indoors. Aging reduces epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol.

Prolonged sun exposure does not cause vitamin D toxicity. Once previtamin D3 accumulates, further UV converts it to inactive photoproducts (lumisterol and tachysterol), and excess cholecalciferol in the skin is also photodegraded. Toxicity therefore comes from excess supplementation or from unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylation, as in granulomatous disease.

blocks.predict: Two people have the same daily sun exposure: one has deeply pigmented skin in Seattle in winter, the other light skin in the same city in summer. Whose serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls, and why does serum calcium change little at first?
blocks.explain: Melanin and low winter UVB both reduce previtamin D3 formation in the first person, so 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls; calcium is defended because lower calcium absorption raises PTH, which increases renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, bone resorption, and renal calcium reabsorption.

sections.title: Barrier lipids, sebum, and dermal glycosaminoglycans

blocks.text: The permeability barrier of the skin lies in the stratum corneum and is often described as bricks and mortar. The bricks are flattened, dead corneocytes filled with keratin and wrapped in a cross-linked protein envelope; the mortar is stacked lipid sheets (lamellae) between them. These lipids come from lamellar bodies, small secretory organelles that form in the stratum spinosum and empty their contents by exocytosis at the junction of the stratum granulosum and stratum corneum.

Lamellar bodies secrete precursors together with the enzymes that process them. Beta-glucocerebrosidase converts glucosylceramides to ceramides, acid sphingomyelinase yields further ceramide from sphingomyelin, and phospholipases release free fatty acids from phospholipids. The finished mixture is roughly equal molar amounts of ceramides, cholesterol, and long-chain free fatty acids. Some ceramides carry an ester-linked linoleic acid that helps hold the lamellae together, which is why essential fatty acid deficiency weakens the barrier (C04). The barrier fails in severe Gaucher disease, in which loss of glucocerebrosidase leaves glucosylceramides unconverted.

Sebum is a different lipid with a different job. Sebaceous glands secrete by the holocrine method, in which whole cells fill with lipid and disintegrate. Androgens drive gland size and output, which explains the rise at puberty. Sebum lubricates hair and skin and adds to surface water resistance. Squalene, a cholesterol precursor, accumulates in sebocytes instead of being converted to cholesterol, and wax esters are also unique to sebum, so both serve as markers of sebaceous lipid. Bacterial lipases from Cutibacterium acnes split triglycerides into free fatty acids on the skin surface.

blocks.title: Barrier lipid versus sebum
rows: Triglycerides (largest share), wax esters, squalene, small amounts of cholesterol and its esters
Prevents water loss and entry of substances
blocks.caption: The barrier holds ceramide, cholesterol, and free fatty acid in near equal molar amounts, with ceramides the largest share by mass; triglycerides dominate sebum.

blocks.text: In the dermis, collagen and elastic fibers sit in a ground substance of glycosaminoglycans that bind large amounts of water and resist compression. Hyaluronic acid is a repeat of glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine; it is the only GAG that is not sulfated and not attached to a core protein, and it is made at the plasma membrane rather than in the Golgi. It is the main water-holding molecule of the dermis and is abundant in loose connective tissue. Dermatan sulfate, a repeat of iduronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine, is the main sulfated GAG of skin. It is carried on the proteoglycan decorin, which binds collagen fibrils and helps control their diameter and spacing. In Hurler and Hunter syndromes, failure to degrade dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate causes thickened skin, and Hunter syndrome can produce pebbly skin papules over the scapulae.

sections.title: Xanthomas as markers of lipoprotein disorders

blocks.text: A xanthoma forms when plasma lipoproteins leak through dermal or tendon capillaries and are taken up by macrophages, which fill with lipid droplets to become foam cells. The amount and type of lipoprotein determine where and how fast deposits form, so the morphology of a xanthoma points to a specific disorder.

Eruptive xanthomas are crops of small yellow papules with a red halo on the buttocks, thighs, and extensor surfaces that appear over days to weeks. They reflect very high triglycerides, typically above about 1,000 mg/dL (about 11 mmol/L), with chylomicrons in the plasma. In familial chylomicronemia (Fredrickson type I), lipoprotein lipase or its activator apoC-II is missing, so chylomicron triglyceride cannot be hydrolyzed in capillary beds. The same chylomicron excess causes milky plasma, lipemia retinalis (creamy white retinal vessels), and acute pancreatitis. Eruptive xanthomas also appear in type V hyperlipidemia and with poorly controlled diabetes, in which insulin deficiency lowers lipoprotein lipase activity. They resolve as triglycerides fall.

Tendon xanthomas are firm nodules in the Achilles tendons and the extensor tendons of the hands. They are a strong sign of familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa), most often from mutations in the LDL receptor gene and less often in apoB-100 or PCSK9. Without receptor-mediated uptake, LDL cholesterol stays high from birth, roughly two to three times normal in heterozygotes and higher still in homozygotes, and LDL enters tendons and the arterial wall. Xanthelasma, soft yellow plaques on the eyelids, also occurs with high LDL, but about half of affected people have normal lipid levels, so it is less specific.

Palmar xanthomas (xanthoma striata palmaris) are yellow deposits in the creases of the palms and fingers and are characteristic of dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III). The apoE2 isoform binds poorly to hepatic remnant receptors, so homozygotes (apoE2/E2) clear chylomicron remnants and IDL slowly. Disease usually appears only with a second factor such as hypothyroidism, obesity, or diabetes, and cholesterol and triglycerides are both raised to similar degrees. Tuberoeruptive xanthomas on the elbows and knees also occur.

blocks.title: Reading a xanthoma
rows: Type I (lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency), type V, uncontrolled diabetes
blocks.caption: Eruptive xanthomas follow triglyceride levels quickly; tendon and palmar xanthomas reflect long-standing cholesterol-rich lipoproteins.

blocks.text: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria. It results from reduced activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), the cytosolic enzyme of heme synthesis that removes four carboxyl groups to convert uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III. Most cases (about 75 to 80%) are sporadic, with normal UROD genes; the rest are familial, with one inherited mutant allele that halves enzyme activity in all tissues. In both forms, symptoms appear only when hepatic UROD activity falls below about 20 to 25% of normal, which requires an added trigger.

The triggers share one mechanism: they increase iron and oxidative stress in hepatocytes. Under those conditions uroporphyrinogen is partly oxidized to uroporphomethene, which inhibits UROD. Alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, smoking, estrogens (oral contraceptives, hormone therapy), and iron overload, often with hemochromatosis gene (HFE) variants, are the classic factors, and most patients have more than one.

steps: Iron and oxidative stress in hepatocytes
Uroporphomethene inhibits hepatic UROD
Uroporphyrinogen accumulates, oxidized to uroporphyrin
Water-soluble porphyrins reach skin through plasma
Porphyrins absorb visible light near 400 nm
Reactive oxygen species damage dermis and basement membrane
Subepidermal blisters, erosions, scarring, milia
blocks.caption: Light, not trauma alone, starts the damage, so lesions are confined to sun-exposed skin.

blocks.text: Uroporphyrinogen and its oxidized form uroporphyrin carry eight carboxyl groups, so they are water soluble and leave in the urine rather than the bile. Absorbing light strongly near 400 nm (the Soret band, visible violet rather than UVB), the excited porphyrin transfers energy to oxygen and generates reactive oxygen species that injure dermal capillaries and the dermal-epidermal junction. Skin on the backs of the hands, forearms, and face becomes fragile, so minor trauma produces erosions and tense subepidermal blisters that heal with scarring and milia (small white keratin cysts). Hypertrichosis over the cheeks and temples, hyperpigmentation, and sclerodermoid plaques are also typical.

PCT has no acute neurovisceral attacks, because the block is late in the pathway, so the neurotoxic precursors aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen are not raised; acute intermittent porphyria (porphobilinogen deaminase) causes attacks without skin lesions. Urine is reddish brown and shows orange-red fluorescence under a Wood lamp, from raised uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin. Liver iron is often increased, and PCT carries a higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

blocks.title: Worked example: why sunscreen fails in PCT
blocks.text: A man with hepatitis C who drinks heavily has blisters and erosions on the backs of his hands despite daily SPF 50 sunscreen. Step 1: two triggers together raise hepatocyte iron and oxidative stress, so uroporphomethene inhibits hepatic UROD past its threshold. Step 2: uroporphyrin accumulates and deposits in the dermis. Step 3: it absorbs visible light near 400 nm, which sunscreens built to block UVB and UVA pass through, so the reactive oxygen species keep forming and the blisters continue. SPF measures UVB protection only.

integration.text: The same skin finding can arise at different levels of organization, and the mechanism tells them apart. Collagen fragility can begin with a missing cofactor (vitamin C), a missing metal transporter (ATP7A in Menkes), a structural gene (type I collagen in osteogenesis imperfecta), or a processing enzyme (Ehlers-Danlos subtypes), and the extra findings point to the level: corkscrew hairs and bleeding gums for diet, kinky hair and neurodegeneration for copper, fractures and blue sclerae for type I collagen. Photosensitivity likewise has two unrelated causes in this chapter: impaired NAD+-dependent repair in pellagra, and photochemical generation of reactive oxygen species by porphyrins in PCT, which is why blisters and scarring belong to PCT and not to pellagra.

The skin also reports on organs far from it. Xanthomas reveal hepatic and capillary lipoprotein handling, PCT reveals hepatic iron and viral infection, vitamin D synthesis links sun exposure to renal hormone production and calcium balance, and periorificial dermatitis can be the first sign of intestinal malabsorption. Skin signs are clues, not proof: zinc and biotin deficiency overlap, xanthelasma often occurs with normal lipids, and laboratory measures such as serum zinc, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, a lipid panel, and urine porphyrins are needed to confirm the mechanism.

summary: Collagen is Gly-X-Y chains hydroxylated in the ER (vitamin C, Fe2+), glycosylated, wound into procollagen, cleaved outside the cell to tropocollagen, and cross-linked by copper-dependent lysyl oxidase.
Scurvy blocks hydroxylation, so collagen is unstable: perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor healing, with normal clotting tests.
Menkes disease (X-linked ATP7A) traps copper in enterocytes, lowering lysyl oxidase and other copper enzymes: kinky hypopigmented hair, fragile vessels, neurodegeneration.
Pellagra is photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia from low NAD+; corn diets, Hartnup disease, carcinoid diversion of tryptophan, and isoniazid-induced B6 loss all reduce niacin.

Vitamin A deficiency causes follicular hyperkeratosis; zinc and biotin cause periorificial dermatitis with alopecia; riboflavin causes angular cheilitis; essential fatty acid loss causes scaly barrier dermatitis.

UVB converts epidermal 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3; liver 25-hydroxylation makes the storage form and regulated renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation makes calcitriol; melanin, latitude, and sunscreen reduce synthesis.

Lamellar bodies supply ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids for the barrier; sebum is mostly triglycerides, wax esters, and squalene; hyaluronic acid and dermatan sulfate hold dermal water and organize collagen.

Eruptive xanthomas mean very high triglycerides (LPL or apoC-II deficiency), tendon xanthomas mean familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor), and palmar crease xanthomas mean dysbetalipoproteinemia (apoE2).

PCT is reduced hepatic UROD activity, triggered by iron, alcohol, hepatitis C, and estrogen; uroporphyrin absorbs visible light and causes blisters, fragility, and hypertrichosis without neurovisceral attacks.
